title: I. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov. In his day Fyodor Pavlovitch was a landowner well known in our district, and people here still remember him for his gloomy, tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago. I will describe it in its proper place. For now I will say only this. This “landowner”—that is what we called him, though he hardly spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange type, yet quite a common one: a man both abject and vicious and, at the same time, senseless. Still, he was one of those senseless men who handle their worldly affairs very well and, it seems, nothing else. Take Fyodor Pavlovitch. He started with next to nothing. His estate was tiny. He ran from one man’s dinner table to another and clung to his hosts as a toady. Yet when he died, it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in cash. And all the while he was one of the most senseless, fantastical fellows in the whole district. I repeat, this was not stupidity. Most of these fantastical fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough. It was just senselessness, and a peculiarly national form of it.

He married twice and had three sons. The eldest, Dmitri, was by his first wife; the other two, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. His first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, belonged to the Miüsovs, a fairly rich and distinguished noble family who were also landowners in our district. How did an heiress, and a beauty too, one of those spirited, clever girls so common in this generation (though found in the last as well), come to marry such a worthless, puny weakling, as we all called him? I won’t try to explain it. I knew a young lady of the last, “romantic” generation. For some years she nursed a mysterious passion for a gentleman whom she could easily have married at any time. Then she invented impossible obstacles to their union. One stormy night she threw herself from a high bank, almost a cliff, into a fairly deep and swift river, and drowned. She did it purely to satisfy her own whim, and to be like Shakespeare’s Ophelia. In fact, if that cliff, her chosen and favorite spot, had been less picturesque, if there had been a dull flat bank instead, the suicide would most likely never have happened. That is a fact, and over the last two or three generations there have probably been quite a few similar cases. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov’s act was no doubt likewise an echo of other people’s ideas, and came from the frustration of having no mental freedom. Perhaps she wanted to show her independence as a woman, to defy class barriers and the tyranny of her family. And her pliable imagination persuaded her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, parasite though he was, was one of the bold, ironical spirits of that progressive age. He was in fact an ill-natured buffoon, nothing more. What gave the marriage its spice was that an elopement came first, and this greatly took Adelaïda Ivanovna’s fancy. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s situation at the time made him especially eager for any such enterprise, since he was desperate to make a career somehow. To attach himself to a good family and win a dowry was a tempting prospect. Of mutual love there was apparently none, neither in the bride nor in him, for all Adelaïda Ivanovna’s beauty. This was perhaps the one case of its kind in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s life, since he was always of a lustful temper and ready to chase after any skirt at the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the only woman who did not appeal particularly to his senses.

Right after the elopement, Adelaïda Ivanovna saw in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. The marriage showed its true face with extraordinary speed. The family got over the shock fairly quickly and handed the runaway bride her dowry. Still, husband and wife settled into a thoroughly disorderly life, with scenes between them all the time. People said the young wife showed far more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch. It is now known that he grabbed all her money, as much as twenty-five thousand roubles, the moment she received it, and those thousands were lost to her for good. For a long time he did all he could to get the little village and the rather fine town house, which were part of her dowry, signed over to himself by some legal deed. He would probably have managed it, simply because she was worn out and wanted to be rid of him, and because his relentless, shameless pestering filled her with contempt and loathing. But luckily Adelaïda Ivanovna’s family intervened and foiled his greed. It is a known fact that the couple often fought. Rumor said, though, that it was not Fyodor Pavlovitch who beat his wife but she who beat him, for she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. At last she left the house and ran off with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a child of three, with her husband. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once filled the house with what amounted to a harem and gave himself up to drunken orgies. Between bouts he would drive all over the province, weeping to anyone who would listen that Adelaïda Ivanovna had left him. He gave details about his married life that were too disgraceful for a husband to tell. What seemed to delight him most and to flatter his vanity was to play the ridiculous role of the injured husband and show off his woes, with embellishments.

“Anyone would think you’d been promoted, Fyodor Pavlovitch, you look so pleased despite your sorrow,” scoffers said to him. Many even added that he was glad to have a new comic part to play the buffoon in, and that he pretended not to see how ludicrous he looked simply to make it funnier. But who knows, it may have been plain simplicity. At last he managed to find out where his runaway wife was. The poor woman, it turned out, was in Petersburg. She had gone there with her divinity student and plunged into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once started bustling around, preparing to go to Petersburg, though for what purpose he could not have said himself. He might really have gone. But once he had decided to go, he felt entitled right away to brace himself for the trip with another bout of reckless drinking. And just then his wife’s family received word that she had died in Petersburg. She had died quite suddenly in a garret. According to one story it was typhus; according to another, starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife’s death. The story goes that he ran out into the street shouting for joy and raising his hands to Heaven: “Lord, now You let Your servant depart in peace.” Others say he wept like a little child, with no restraint at all, so that people felt sorry for him, repulsive as he was. Quite possibly both versions were true: he rejoiced at being set free, and at the same time wept for the woman who had freed him. As a rule, people, even wicked ones, are far more naïve and simple-hearted than we suppose. And we ourselves are, too.
